title: Tropic Thunder
full_review:
It must have seemed like a good premise on paper, and someday this satiric misfire may find a cult following, but for now let it be said "Tropic Thunder" (DreamWorks) seems a major disappointment.

 

Relentlessly vulgar and only fitfully funny, this schizophrenic action comedy focuses on a group of washed-up and insecure movie actors: action star Tugg Speedman (Ben Stiller), coming off a box-office flop in a "serious" role as a mentally-challenged man (a "retard" in the film's non-PC jargon); gross-out comedy star -- and heavy drug addict -- Jeff Portnoy (Jack Black); pretentious multiple Oscar-winning Aussie Kirk Lazurus (Robert Downey Jr.), who's dyed his skin to play an African-American role; hip-hop star turned thespian Alpa Chino (Brandon T. Jackson); and rookie Kevin Sandusky (Jay Baruchel), who come together for the titular big budget war movie in Vietnam.

 

When the multimillion-dollar set is accidentally blown to smithereens, the aborted film's director, Damien Cockburn (Steve Coogan), refuses to accept that the film is canceled, and takes his actors deep into the jungle to continue shooting in the wild.

They are soon targeted by a gang of ruthless heroin dealers, who mistake them for U.S. drug enforcement agents. Shortly after proclaiming that he's Jesus Christ in a moment of sacrilegious bravado, Cockburn steps on an old land mine and he's blown into bits for real. The deluded Speedman insists it's all an illusion and, picking up the decapitated head, licks the blood, typical of the in-your-face humor on display.

Eventually, the others lose confidence in Speedman and split off on their own. But when captured by a guerrilla gang led by a seriously vicious 12-year-old (Brandon Skoo Hoo), Speedman finally realizes his predicament, and his friends decide they'll rescue him.

Stiller and Black are in standard form, and despite the outrageousness of the conceit, Downey scores comic points as an actor with major identity issues who has totally morphed into his African-American role, much to the disdain of the group's genuine black member.

The game cast also includes Matthew McConaughey as Speedman's agent, single-mindedly obsessed with a contract detail guaranteeing his client TiVo on location, and Tom Cruise in a flamboyantly eccentric turn as ruthless Hollywood honcho Lee Grossman: bald, bearded, bespectacled, and foulmouthed in the extreme! Nick Nolte and Danny McBride are on hand as, respectively, the real-life Vietnam hero impersonated by Speedman in the movie, and the film's explosives expert.

There are some sharp jibes here and there (Stiller, Justin Theroux and Etan Cohen co-wrote the script), but nothing quite equals the five fake -- and intentionally outrageous -- trailers that open the film, allegedly showing the stars in their typical roles. These include, by the way, a Dan Brown-like potboiler called "Satan's Alley," with Lazarus as a medieval monk in a "forbidden" relationship (cameo by Tobey Maguire), replete with portentous music and narration.

Yet, this frenetic spoof never succeeds in reconciling its uncertain tone between Hollywood sendup and genuinely brutal adventure.

The film contains nonstop rough language and profanity, crass expressions, strong violence and gore, torture, brief irreverence, drug use, scatological humor and frank sexual references. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
